en: His eyes blazing with rage,
As though he would camp along the Seven Valleys,
As though he would swallow the whole world,
His lion's eyes blazed,
I have poured away much of my strength,
I have made a stake of my arm,
I have spilled my blood by the spoonful.
To this blackhearted bloodthirsty man
I shall now sacrifice
My precious life, no greater than a fly.
I shall ask his inmost secret,
And if he will not tell it,
My wrath shall rise till I stand rigid,
And I shall do something to this bloodthirsty man.
Why should I go on living as a slave;
What else remains for me to do?”
So saying, Külchoro
Drew a line as a sign;
The poor falcon among men
Was about to do something extraordinary.
He was about to begin disaster,
About to inflame the madness,
That incurable, festering wound.
He was about to bring upon the hero
A calamity no man had ever seen.
Refusing to release the young man,
He was about to tear his mind apart.
Standing rigid in his rage,
He held fast to his lord,
The dear one who had made him helpless.
How could he ever release
That man whose stature loomed like a mountain?
Allah Most High indeed creates
His servants in every form.
Some souls He made heroes,
Some He made lionhearted warriors,
Some souls He made deficient,
And some souls the Creator made
Equal to the dark grave.
Then Külchoro,
Clashing and refusing to let go,
Clung to the bloodthirsty lion.
He began circling through his speech,
Hurling out forceful words,
Each word's ending
Devouring anyone who understood.
Heedless of your vastness,
Showing mercy to no living soul,
Heedless of the blessed lion,
The poor hero who had endured many ordeals
Did not spare his threadlike life.
“Why does he stand there without speaking?
Why does God strike
This witless, bloodthirsty sultan?” he said.
“For this I have been diminished,
Yet he gives no thought to me;
For this I was taken into slavery,
Yet he does not grieve for me at all.
I spent my precious youth,
And made a club of my head.”
When Külchoro and Kara Döö together seized Semetey, saying, “Now that I have caught you,
I shall not leave you alive but kill you,” Külchoro grew angry and said, “Neither entering
The grave in death nor living among your people, you made me bear your torment. Now,
If I do not kill you and then die myself, unless you renounce the life of this world, speak
A word to me, or come to your senses”—and in his fury Külchoro seized his lord,
Shaking him and refusing to let go. Then Semetey, frightened by Külchoro's voice,
Began to speak:
He seized him and twisted his mouth,
Standing rigid in his rage,
And spoke to him harshly.
As he spoke so harshly,
At that moment Semetey
Quietly began speaking weighty words:
“It is indeed true that you were parted
And left without the one dear to you.
You were a man whose glory loomed like a mountain,
And it is also true that, parted from your noble one,
You were left humiliated.
The sable cap upon one's head—
Who would not wear it at a jaunty tilt?
While fortune rests upon one's head,
Who would not stride about thundering?
You were parted and separated,
Enduring shame and grieving.
What you have said is indeed true;
I was the one who escaped alive
And became separated from you.
Whenever even a faint cry is heard,
My troubled heart is torn.
Its angry force
Seems like Külchoro's.
That hero Külchoro of yours
Was a man apart from all others.
Crackling like lightning,
Such was the power of his voice.
Whenever he shouted, ‘Uncle!’
His cry carried far.
A doe with her fawn,
At the sound of the hero's voice,
Unable to withstand its venom,
Would miscarry her young.
Some would collapse and die,
While those that survived
Would waste their days in sickness.
My surging heart is torn;
That furious shouted cry
Sounds like Külchoro's voice.
If you seize me, you may hold me,
You may offer me as a sacrifice.
You may simply kill this soul
And utterly destroy it.
Your courage is lofty and your wrath is strong,
You lay low whoever challenges you.”
The noble lord spoke these words,
Saying as follows:
“O my child, what you say is also true.
You have a black and unyielding nature,
And fearful words of wrath;
You strike down whoever crosses you,
And gnaw whoever encounters you.
You set dry grass ablaze upon the ground
And burn the meadows;
Such was your day as the hero Külchoro.
When I look upon your radiance,
It bears the terror of a dragon.
When your cry is heard,
It has the voice of a lion.
If you kill me, you will surely kill me,
If you grow fierce, you will swallow me.
And if your rage seizes you again,
You will utterly finish me.
You are indeed a hero and a lion,
I recognize you by your voice:
You are Külchoro himself.
You are the falcon's dark eye.
When you grapple and lay hands upon a foe,
No man's strength can overcome you,
Nor can a lion's teeth pierce you.
Champion among the valley's heroes,
Mightiest of the falcons,
Favored among the blessed.
All in all,
You are the Morning Star of heroic lions.
My heart trembles and is torn;
That fearsome battle cry
Seems just like Külchoro's.
If you are Külchoro,
Then it is also true that you are a khan.
That my honor once bore a great duty,
And that I still exist, are also true.
That fire has swept through my core
And consumed it is also true.
Wailing and sobbing uncontrollably,
From the sky came a six-fold hailstorm,
A driving sleet.
Choking every ditch,
A torrential rain brought down the night,
And just as it stood thus,
I saw a beauty among women,
With a thimble mouth and camel-calf eyes,
Roving eyes like a camel calf’s,
A crimson dress and slender waist,
Slanting, gleaming eyes,
I saw an extraordinarily beautiful girl.
Her attendants were seven thousand,
Her armored warriors eighty-four,
They cast spells by reciting their book,
Never among humankind had I seen such a beauty.
She threw my blood into turmoil,
And from all mortal men
She took away my strength.
She made my eyes unable to see,
Thus she transformed me.
She made my ears deaf,
Eighty sorceress maidens
Surrounded me three times each day.
They led me astray from the road,
No human shape remained to me.
If you saw it, such is the calamity;
She bewitched me beyond measure.
Can Bakai still be alive,
He who always found wise counsel?
Aichürök’s younger sister,
The fairy’s daughter Kökmonchok,
Has bewitched me grievously,
Bringing night over my eyes,
Never ceasing to beguile my soul,
She has spilled much of my blood.
She keeps barring my road,
Binding my hands with spells,
Stripping the coat from my back,
Bewitching me utterly—
My colt, through sorcery I took a wife.
My mind is greatly distracted,
But when I gather all my courage,
Your voice seems to be Külchoro’s.
I cannot leave my words unspoken;
Keep watch over me.
When all forty attacked,
When I was parted from the gray steed
And left upon the open plain.
Yesterday, when I slipped away to the white tomb,
Jaw sprang forth beneath jaw,
Kanchoro the swine emerged as a foe,
Tongue sprang forth beneath tongue,
He readied his sword tight in its scabbard,
Not one remaining behind, all alone
The people of Jediger rode out,
And the black stallion, the fleet racer,
The foal of the miraculous gray,
The carved beauty taken as spoil,
The cudgel inherited from Toltoy,
When Surkön could no longer go.
The teeming black host of Jediger
Drew their bows like falling rain,
And shot their strange arrows like hailstones;
The foe surged roaring like a flood,
The raiders overran the land,
And when the enemy came roaring,
There was no luck anywhere in me;
Parted from Taibuurul,
Your princely uncle had no fortune.
When Surkön could go no farther,
I seized both his forelock
And his ears together.
To follow my father Manas’s path,
I dedicated him and slaughtered him.
In the blink of an eye,
Before one could turn this way or that,
Clouds arose from the hollows,
And over the summits of the mountains
Black clouds closed in,
The grass shook and quivered,
The princes fled in panic,
But is there any reason to flee?
Ah, ill-fated children, where are the people?
Will the day come when we reach them?
I sing and tell my song,
I tell my secret as truly as my faith.
My father’s confidant,
The lion Bakai, his comrade—
Can my grandsire still be safe and living?
Seize Kanchoro,
O wise man whose eyes have seen much,
Who has surpassed so many rivals.
A herald grown old among the people,
A saint from ancient times,
Whose valor is unlike another’s,
My heroic uncle Bakai,
My grandsire, elder of the people,
Has medicine in his pouch,
And all things beyond what others possess;
He has yet another remedy.
One medicine is called “Eбep,”
In dear Bakai’s hands
It used to soothe the aching place;
